ratings.rationale: Unauthenticated fabricated emissions create false targets. ADS-B injection has practical experimental support, but LEO-specific reception and integrity consequences remain analogue. Cross-checking may detect inconsistencies; a fabricated, internally consistent target can evade it.
ratings.issue: A1.1 alone is incomplete: observable reports and the receiver's acceptance of fabricated emissions are also relevant.

ratings.rationale: Replay makes previously genuine content appear current at a different time or location. It is distinct from generating new identities. Temporal plausibility and track consistency may detect it, but no inherent freshness authentication is specified.
ratings.issue: Replay detection depends on track history and association policy, neither of which is specified sufficiently.

ratings.rationale: The aircraft's broadcast position is tampered with while independently measured arrival geometry remains genuine. This is a genuine deception scenario, but the independent cross-check should normally expose the discrepancy. The cited evidence does not establish a general bypass.
ratings.issue: The claimed masking chain is unspecified. A false broadcast position alone is not equivalent to a false independent multilateration position.

ratings.rationale: In-band interference prevents reception and decoding, producing coverage degradation. ADS-B interference has experimental support. Receiver-level interference monitoring can identify degradation independently of the later multilateration solution.
ratings.issue: The affected footprint and resulting regional user count are not quantified; RF interference detection is assumed rather than specified.

ratings.rationale: Coordinated emissions can create an apparently coherent false multilateration source. Published terrestrial multilateration research supports the general mechanism. AOA and independent ADS-B consistency checks are important but do not guarantee detection.
ratings.issue: The angular-resolution qualification is central and needs explicit treatment; terrestrial multilateration evidence does not establish LEO feasibility.

ratings.rationale: The distinguishing consequence is displacement of an existing genuine track rather than creation of a ghost. Coordinated multilateration spoofing provides analogue support. Strong-pass checks may detect sufficiently large single-satellite biases but do not establish detection of coordinated manipulation.
ratings.issue: Substantially overlaps T1.05. Distinction requires demonstrating takeover of an existing identity and track rather than merely creating a false target.

ratings.rationale: Selective reception denial is distinct from footprint-wide jamming because it targets chosen aircraft or beams. Missing reception can be detected through coverage and track-continuity monitoring. Evidence for the precise satellite-array mechanism is limited.
ratings.issue: The cited instrument-landing-system interference research is not direct evidence of selective 1090ES satellite reception denial.

ratings.rationale: Excessive receptions can degrade decoding and processing capacity, causing regional measurement loss. The general resource-exhaustion concept is credible, but the cited LEO network studies do not directly demonstrate 1090ES payload saturation.
ratings.issue: The cited studies concern LEO network security, not necessarily RF receiver or ADS-B decoder saturation. Separate RF and processor exhaustion mechanisms.

ratings.rationale: The threat modifies genuine measured observables before timestamping, distinct from later report or clock manipulation. Doppler-based verification research supports related measurement-integrity concerns, but the combined TOA, FOA and AOA attack surface remains insufficiently established.
ratings.issue: Multipath, frequency interference and array manipulation are different mechanisms and should not be treated as one demonstrated attack.

ratings.rationale: GNSS denial removes one clock-disciplining input and can degrade holdover. It is primarily denial, not tau, because the immediate effect is loss of an input rather than an imposed time offset. Aviation incidents establish GNSS interference, not satellite-clock impact.
ratings.issue: Ground-based interference against a satellite GNSS receiver requires a credible link-budget and antenna-visibility justification. Aircraft GNSS incidents are only analogue evidence.

ratings.rationale: The defining effect is a persistent onboard time-reference offset. It remains possible with authenticated messages, satisfying the tau invariance test. GNSS spoofing has experimental support, while satellite-clock consequences and LEO-specific stealth remain extrapolations.
ratings.issue: The record omits the second clock input: PTP may constrain or expose the GNSS-induced offset. The 100 ns assumption needs system-specific validation.

ratings.rationale: Insufficient command authentication permits unauthorised control of the satellite platform and potentially hosted payload functions. On-orbit security experiments support the general risk. Consequences can include denial, firmware modification or measurement manipulation.
ratings.issue: The hosted-payload and clock-control edges are inferred, not established. Separate command authentication failure from the resulting privilege and payload compromise.

ratings.rationale: Memory-safety exploitation is a distinct software vulnerability class that can produce privileged execution and persistent platform compromise. Satellite software security experiments provide relevant analogue support. Consequences depend on reachable interfaces and software architecture.
ratings.issue: The reachable command-path assumption is not demonstrated. Memory-safety exploitation and its impact should be separated from generic software compromise.

ratings.rationale: Firmware alteration or boot-chain compromise establishes persistent malicious behaviour and differs from exploiting a runtime memory defect. Satellite and satellite-terminal security research supports the broader firmware-integrity concern.
ratings.issue: Combines physical fault injection, update-path compromise and secure-boot bypass. These have different prerequisites and should be distinguished.

ratings.rationale: Compromising ground-station terminals provides control over downlink reception or command transmission. SATCOM terminal research supports this general exposure. The principal effect is loss or manipulation of ground connectivity rather than direct alteration of onboard measurements.
ratings.issue: The terminal's management plane and its relationship to the mission network are unspecified. The L1 assignment obscures the ground-management and link-layer entry points.

ratings.rationale: Ground-station reception denial interrupts report delivery or command connectivity. The LEO network denial literature supports general network-level availability concerns, but direct evidence for the specified ground RF mechanism is limited. Link monitoring should expose outages.
ratings.issue: RF interference and resource exhaustion are separate mechanisms. The cited simulator and LEO network research do not establish ground-station antenna susceptibility.

missing_threats.title: Phased-array beamforming and calibration compromise
missing_threats.why: Calibration or beamforming integrity loss can systematically bias AOA and degrade localisation without external RF interference.

missing_threats.title: Payload extraction and measurement firmware compromise
missing_threats.why: Compromised extraction firmware can falsify TOA, FOA and AOA measurements independently of bus-level compromise.

missing_threats.title: Onboard oscillator degradation or manipulation
missing_threats.why: Drift, ageing, temperature sensitivity and oscillator manipulation can undermine timing even when GNSS and PTP inputs remain available.

missing_threats.title: GNSS-to-PTP timing-source disagreement
missing_threats.why: Conflicting time sources, faulty source selection or common-mode dependencies can produce undetected timing degradation.

missing_threats.title: Payload thermal or radiation-induced measurement degradation
missing_threats.why: Environmental faults can cause correlated measurement and timing degradation, challenging integrity assumptions and availability.

rubric_ambiguities: The STRONG and WEAK detection assumptions explicitly concern single-satellite timing bias, not other threats; their applicability to unrelated threats is unclear.
The D rubric combines regional denial and flagged degradation, although their operational consequences and affected-user populations differ.
Analogue-only evidence is unclear when terrestrial ADS-B experiments demonstrate the exact RF protocol but not the LEO receiver architecture.
The Affected users dimension describes root-event extent, but does not define how to count aircraft, footprints or constellation-wide events.
A threat with several possible consequences has no explicit rule for choosing D when the most severe consequence requires additional compromise.
batch_comments.overall: The batch covers important L1 attack surfaces but frequently extrapolates terrestrial ADS-B, terrestrial multilateration and generic satellite-security experiments to LEO-MLAT-B without demonstrating architectural equivalence. T1.05 and T1.06 overlap substantially, while T1.12-T1.14 require clearer separation of initial access, vulnerability exploitation and persistent compromise. Timing-source diversity, AOA integrity and payload firmware trust deserve additional attention. The numerical detectability scores should not be treated as established without explicit detection predicates for each threat.
